Those such as the Pātañjala-Haṭhayogins and the Pūrvamīmāṃsakas who were intent on refuting [this].

Lord Bhairava, however, in order to bestow grace upon his devotees, [manifests] through a stream characterized by the fourfold speech beginning with Parā and Paśyantī, which consists of the nature of vibration (spanda), is designated by the term "Rājayoga," and is composed of the union of the powers of knowledge and action.

Desiring that [the disciple] should attain the expansion of the phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, and wishing to instruct him on the path known as the "Supreme" (*anuttara*), which consists of knowledge and action, [the author] introduces the subject through the introduction of Bhairavī’s question. And thus says the Śruti: "Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. In the cave..."
"Three [parts] are deposited and do not stir; humans speak the fourth of speech.
Thus [spoke] the venerable Bhairavī: "O Lord, how is the unsurpassed [teaching] that immediately bestows Kaulika-siddhi?"
By the mere knowledge of which, one shall attain equality with the Khecarī. || 1 ||
O Lord, "Anuttara" means that there exists nothing superior to it; therefore, it is the unsurpassed reality consisting of the mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*).
It bestows *kaulikīsiddhi*—that which arises in the *kula*, namely the body—and grants identity with consciousness (*cidaikātmya*). Such is the *kaulikīsiddhi*, which belongs even to the insentient.
Jīvanmukti is the firm realization of the identity of the body and so forth with Consciousness alone.
And it has been said:
"Even while the body and other such things are being perceived as objects of thought, the firm realization of their identity with Consciousness alone is jīvanmukti."

(Śaktisūtra 16) "How" means in what manner; "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) means at the very moment of full realization. The meaning is: "Tell me that means (*upāya*), by the mere experience of which this person attains equality with the *khecarī*."

The meaning is that one becomes liberated when one attains the state of equality—characterized by absolute freedom—with your powers (śaktis), which are of the nature of pure consciousness and move through the void (khecarīs). || 1 ||
O Lord, tell me this secret, the great secret:
that power which resides in the heart, the Kaulikī, the Mistress of the Kula.
Tell that to me, O Lord of Gods, so that I may attain satisfaction.

Even though this is a secret to be guarded, and even more than that a great secret, a most profound secret, O Lord, O You whose nature is to manifest— nevertheless, speak it to me, who am non-different from You, and enlighten me with articulate speech.

It is for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees. As for the definition of *vaikharī* speech, it is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "When the breath has been expanded in the [articulatory] locations, *vaikharī* speech—which assumes the form of phonemes—is dependent upon the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of speakers."

Thus: "Likewise, O Lord, tell me by its very nature that power which resides in the heart—the *cicchakti* situated in the heart, the *kaulikī*, the pervader of the body and so forth, the mistress of the *kula*, the mistress of the body (*kula*), who brings about identity with consciousness; by hearing which I may attain satisfaction and freedom from longing."
Śrī Bhairava said: Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to that which is even higher than the highest.
O Goddess, this Kaulika rite resides within the space of my heart; O Mistress of the Gods, I shall now describe it, for it bestows immediate Kaulika perfection.

O Goddess! Listen now to that unsurpassed and supreme nature, which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), even of the supreme light (*citprakāśa*). This method is the Kaulika means (*upāya*), which effects the realization of the identity with pure consciousness (*cidekarūpatā*) of the inert body and so forth, just as fire produces the state of being fire in a lump of iron.

However, until now this method has not been asked about by anyone; therefore, it remains only within the sky of my heart and has not been revealed externally. I shall now speak—that is, I declare—the means which bestows the *kaulika* accomplishment and establishes the identity of the body and so forth with consciousness. || 4 ||
He begins to explain that very point:
"Now, all the vowels ending with the bindu are the initial lunar days (tithis);
within them, through the conjunction of time, the Moon and the Sun are proclaimed. (5)

Now, "atha" (then) refers to the beginning; the first fifteen phonemes, starting with 'a' and ending with the nasal bindu (the letter 'aṃ'), are the vowels known as the *tithis* (lunar days). Within them—that is, in the midst of the pronunciation of those phonemes—there occurs, through the conjunction of time (*kālayogena*), that which is called "time" (*kāla*), meaning the power of subtle activity (*kalanā*). Through its conjunction...

Since it has been stated that consciousness first transforms into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through their connection, the moon and the sun are proclaimed as the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and are declared to be the causes of activity. Furthermore—

The lunar days, beginning with the first (pratipad), proceed through the conjunctions and disjunctions of the sun and moon and by connection with time; this is the external meaning, which is both allusive and easy to understand. || 5 ||
Now, he begins to explain how the phonemes (varṇas) possess the nature of everything by virtue of being the signified and the signifier:
"O lady of excellent vows, the principles beginning with earth and ending with the Puruṣa reside respectively within the phonemes beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma'."

The Śiva-tattva consists of the letters from *a* to the visarga (*ḥ*). The five elements (*bhūta-pañcaka*) consist of the letters from *ka* to *ṅa*, beginning with earth and ending with space. The five subtle elements (*tanmātra-pañcaka*) consist of the letters from *ca* to *ña*, beginning with smell and ending with sound. The five organs of action (*karmendriya-pañcaka*) consist of the letters from *ṭa* to *ṇa*, beginning with the feet and ending with speech. [The five organs of perception consist of the letters] from *ta* to *na*, beginning with the sense of smell...

The five sense organs beginning with hearing and ending with the intellect (dhī), and the group of five beginning with the feet and ending with the mind, known as mind, ego, intellect, primordial nature (prakṛti), and the person (puruṣa). || 6 ||
There is a fourfold set of meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) on air, fire, water, and earth;
above that, the group beginning with 'śa' is renowned as the five Brahmans mentioned previously.

The four [elements] beginning with *ya*— namely, the *vāyavī*, *āgneyī*, *vāruṇī*, *aindrī*, and (*pārthivī*) *dhāraṇā*s— are the designations for their respective locations; above those are the five Brahmans of the five [elements] beginning with *śa*, renowned as Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta.

It should be stated: the tactile sensation (*sparśa*) that follows the persistence of the *sattva* aspect of the *paśyantī* state; the form (*rūpa*), the taste (*rasa*), and the smell (*gandha*); the meditation on the *praṇava* in the form of the Sun pervading the body, which is the *pārthivī-dhāraṇā*;
and [the purification] of the external and internal body by the flames of the *kālāgni* (time-fire) arising from the big toe of the right foot.

The meditation on [the body] having become ashes is the fiery (āgneyī) [purification]; the meditation on the bodily ashes being dispersed in the ten directions by a fierce wind is the airy (vāyavī); the meditation on that location being washed by the nectar of Śakti fallen from the *dvādaśānta* is the watery (āpyā); then, [there is the meditation] on the individual soul (*jīva*) residing in the ether together with Kuṇḍalinī.
The descent [of the deity] into the heart by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and the nectar is the *vāruṇī-dhāraṇā*.
That [creation] should be known as "rootless" (amūlā) according to its sequence; it is declared to be the creation of the vowels (kṣāntā).

The creation of phonemes (varṇasṛṣṭi), from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, occurs according to the sequence of phonemes. It is said that "rootless" means having the letter *a* as its root—that is, having the letter *a* as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). This is because the letter *a* consists of the nature of all phonemes.
The Śruti says:
"The letter 'a' is indeed all speech; this very [letter], being manifested by the consonants (sparśas) and sibilants (ūṣmans), becomes many and takes on various forms."
Thus it is said. In the *Gītā* as well:
"Among letters, I am the letter 'A'... (10.33). For instance, the self-reflection (*vimarśa*) of the Supreme Lord is 'A', and therein lies the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*), which is 'Ā'.

*Pūrṇecchā* (the will of fullness) is *i*; the will tending toward knowledge is *ī*; knowledge tending toward the unfolding of being (*bhāva*) is *u*; that same [knowledge], diminished by the contraction of supreme consciousness (*anuttarasaṃvit*), is *ū*;
that very [consciousness], as if becoming void through the forgetting of its own nature and turned outward, is *ṝ* and *ṛ*; and through the attainment of motionless voidness, it is *ḷ* and *ḹ*.

Thus, this tetrad, through the attainment of emptiness (*śūnyatva*), is described as having the nature of a neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*), like a burnt seed; yet, there is not an absolute departure from its status as a seed. Furthermore, when *Anuttara* and *Ānanda* are joined with *Icchā* and *Īśana* respectively, [the result is] *E*.
And it has been said:

According to the rule *avarṇa-ivarṇe e* (Kātantra-vṛtti 1.2.2), when that very form [the vowel *a*] merges with *ai*, it becomes *ai*; likewise, *a ā u ū o* becomes *a ā o*, and *au*. This should also be stated regarding the opening (*unmeṣa*). Thus, when Will (*icchā*) and Knowledge (*jñāna*) dissolve into the Absolute (*anuttara*), remaining as nothing but the Point (*bindu*), it becomes *aṃ*; that indeed is [the state].

The Supreme Lord, by virtue of being primarily characterized by the emission (*visarga*) of Śakti, is "Aḥ. The sixteenfold digit (*kalā*), which consists of the reflective power (*vimarśa-śakti*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, extending from the Earth element up to Śakti, is thus celebrated.
And it has been said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"In the person consisting of sixteen parts, they call that the supreme part.

Thus, the density of the vowel *a* is the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) because it is guttural; likewise, the *ca*-group (*cavarga*) belongs to the vowel *i* because it is palatal, the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) to the vowel *u* because it is labial, and the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*) to the vowel *ṛ*.

Because the *ḷ* sound is palatal (*mūrdhanya*), the dental class (*tavarga*) belongs to it; because the *ya* and *śa* sounds are at the end of the palatal class (*cavarga*), the *ra* and *ṣa* sounds belong to the retroflex class (*ṭavarga*), and the *la* and *sa* sounds belong to the dental class (*tavarga*).

The letter *va* is also half-nasal for the *ta* and *pa* classes. Thus, even though the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*) is formless, its very nature is that of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). The vowels consist of the seed-syllables of Śiva, while the consonants are the form of Śakti.

The letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, which abide within the intellect (*mati*), are called the "source" (*yoni*); thus, the condensation of phonemes abiding in the body of the supreme speech (*aparāvāk*) becomes manifest in the form of *vaikharī*. || 8 ||
Of all mantras and vidyās indeed, O illustrious one. (8)
This source (yoni) is proclaimed in every way throughout all tantras;
it is the primordial creation of the phonemes, ending with *kṣa*, the source that is the cause of origination. And it has been said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
In her own glory consisting of reflection,
she is the protection against the fear of her own contraction;
she has swallowed up all conceptual constructions of the universe.
Some inexplicable experience is the meaning of the word "mantra."
Thus [ends the eighth].
(p. 7) Now he explains the extraction of the Great Mantra:
"O auspicious lady, it is joined with the fourteenth [vowel] and endowed with the end of the Lord of the lunar days. (9)
O lady of beautiful hips, the third Brahman is the heart of the Bhairava-self.

It consists of three syllables, "A-gho-ra," existing among the vowels. That which is called the third Brahman, named Aghora, is conjoined with—that is, connected to—the fourteenth vowel; that is the letter *a*. The fifteenth vowel is the lunar day (*tithi*).

The letter *aṃ* is joined with that [letter] which is peaceful (*śānta*) and the last of the *śa*-group, namely *dva*; by means of that, there arises the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) "I" (*aham*),
which is of the nature of the stage of *paśyantī*,
as stated in the *Vākyapadīya*:
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all sequential order withdrawn;
it is the inner light of its own nature, the subtle speech that never departs.
Thus characterized, [it is said]:
"That which is supreme is Brahman alone.
By this statement, [the reference is] to the light of consciousness (citprakāśa), whose nature is the supreme word (parāvāk), which is Bhairava himself, and which is all-pervasive.

The heart is the great mantra that constitutes the essence. According to the rule *tithī kṛdikārād aktinaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.45), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied; thus, for example, the word *rajanī*. And it has been said:
"The repose of light within itself is indeed proclaimed to be the state of 'I-ness' (*ahaṃbhāva*)" (Āgamaprāmāṇya 22).
Thus:
"That is the throbbing, the Great Beingness...
and so forth.
And as it is said: "The heart of the Supreme Lord" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.14). Likewise:
"They know the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) to be the very nature of manifestation; otherwise [it would be nothing]."
"Though luminous and colored by objects, it is like an insentient crystal and the like" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.11).

Furthermore, the third Brahman is the Aghora mantra; conjoined with the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cit*), it is the heart of Svacchandabhairava, whose nature is Bhairava—the great mantra that constitutes his very essence. 9.
One who is not born of a Yoginī and is not Rudra certainly does not obtain this. || 10 ||

The Heart of the God of Gods, which immediately bestows liberation through yoga—this supreme Heart, which consists of the reflective awareness of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), is the essence of all that is knowable; it is a certain secret reality. It is not clearly manifest to one who is not Rudra—that is, to one born as a class other than a Yoginī.

He attains [it], yet he does not attain it. Furthermore, that portion of Rudra who is not yet destined for the state of Bhairava does not attain it. "Clearly" means: by suppressing the identification with the body and through the predominance of consciousness, that which he attains is the portion of Rudra born as a Yoginī, whose state of Bhairava is imminent; at the very moment of attainment, it is immediate.

"Yoga-vimokṣada" means that it bestows yoga and liberation; "yoga" is the absorption into the conscious Self (cidātman), and "liberation" is the state of being composed solely of consciousness. Thus it gives these.
Having uttered the speech of the *paśyantī* level, he describes its greatness:
"When this [mantra] is properly uttered, the great multitude of mantras and mudrās [is attained]. (11)
Immediately, it attains the state of being that very [deity's] face, which is the characteristic of the penetration of one's own body.

This occurs through the continuous recitation (*uccāra*) and contemplative reflection (*parāmarśa*) upon this great mantra characterized as "I" (*aham*), as well as upon the Aghora mantra, by means of constant identification with each respective deity. Thus, it is "perfectly" [achieved].

When [the practice] is performed with consciousness as the primary focus, preceded by the forgetting of the sense of "I" in the body, the great multitude of mantras and mudrās—the entire assembly of mantra-deities—immediately, at the very moment of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), comes face-to-face with that yogin; how so? By means of the characteristic of entering one's own body—that is, the body of the yogin.
The possession (*āveśa*) of the deities is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); it is the mark (*lakṣma*) found when one attains their presence. || 11 ||
(p. 9) Now, he describes the power [attained] through the correct application of meditative concentration (samādhi):
"But he who, sealed by the *cummaka*, remembers [it] for even a moment... (12).
Then that person binds together the entire multitude of mantras and mudrās;
when questioned, he even speaks of matters past and future.

That yogi who, marked— that is, bound— by the "kisser" (cumbaka), which is the touch of Śakti, continuously remembers the conscious self for a moment or two (muhūrta) and reflects upon it as "I am," that very person [attains] the host of mantras and mudrās— the assembly of deities belonging to both mantras and mudrās— at that time.

He connects with and perceives directly through the relationship of possessor and possessed; thus, when he emerges from that state and is questioned by someone regarding his own or the world's auspicious or inauspicious matters, he declares past and future objects— that is,
purposes separated by the times of the past and the future— and his speech does not [fail].
The meaning is that it deviates. || 13 ||
While reciting whatever form of the deity is intended at the beginning of the watch [of the night],
one sees it directly and without doubt, drawn forth by the powers of Rudra.

The ablative case in "praharāt" is used in the sense of the elision of a verbal suffix (lyablope); that is, having presided over the conscious self (cidātmā) in the form of the deity for the duration of a single watch (praharamātram), the yogi established in samādhi, while reciting and contemplating,
whatever intended or desired form of a deity— such as Indra or another— there may be, becomes that very form of the deity.
Without doubt, he directly perceives that which has been drawn forth and awakened by the powers of Rudra—the supreme lordly powers such as Brāhmī and the others. || 14 ||
By remembering [this] for merely two watches (six hours), one becomes established in the sky;
by three watches, all the Mothers, the powerful mistresses of yoga, [appear]. 15.
The heroes, the lords of heroes, the perfected ones, and the powerful host of Śākinīs, having arrived and received their pledge, were impelled by Bhairava. (16)
They bestow supreme accomplishment or whatever fruit is desired.

If the yogi, resting in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), remains mindful for two *praharas*, he becomes situated in space and attains the power of moving through the air (*khagati*) due to his rest in absorption; if he rests in absorption for three *praharas*, then—
Having received the command from Bhairavanātha, the Mothers— Brāhmī and the others—
who perform the fivefold acts, as well as the heroes (vīras), yogins, lords of heroes (vīreśvaras), sovereigns of yogins (yogīndras),
and the perfected ones (siddhas) such as Kapila, along with the host of Śaktis and the assembly of Yoginīs, [attacked] him who remained in meditative absorption for three watches of the night.

Having approached the yogin, they will grant him supreme, perfect accomplishment (*siddhi*), as well as any other desired fruit— that is, the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) characterized by the power to employ his own nature as he pleases. || 16 ||
By this, the accomplished ones have attained success, and the practitioners of mantra will attain it and cause others to attain it. || 17 ||
Whatever is found in the Bhairava Tantra, all of that is accomplished through this very means—
through this samādhi characterized by resting in consciousness-bliss (cidānanda) and through the Aghora mantra. By means of these,
perfected yogins become autonomous in choosing either worldly existence or liberation, and they accomplish their goals.

They will also bring about other accomplishments (*siddhis*). Likewise, whatever fruit has been declared in the *Bhairava-tantra* for this very practitioner of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*), all of that is accomplished through this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consisting of the worship of the Great Mantra and through the *aghora-mantra*. || 17 ||
Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, if he knows even a little according to reality, [is likewise empowered]. || 18 ||

He shall always possess accomplishment; he is a yogi and he is initiated— whosoever knows the Great Mantra in this manner, that is, in reality, by transcending the sense of "I" regarding the body and setting aside the authority pertaining to the divisions of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).

Thus, even though he has not seen the mandala, that circle of deities consisting of the mandala, the jar-sacrifice (kalaśayāga), and so forth, which is employed in the ritual of initiation— even if unperceived by him— he, being of such a nature, becomes a possessor of accomplishment (siddhi),
a perpetual yogi, and one who is initiated. And it is said:
The thorough knowledge of one's own true nature is this mantra, which is ultimate;
it is this initiation, this yoga, and the unsurpassed even among ritual actions. (p. 11)
Thus: the yoga known as Navanābha consists of the accomplishment of the vessel (*kalaśa*), the mandala, and the fire (*agni*); the preparation of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*);

the purification of the disciple; the procedure for ritual placement (*nyāsa*); the purification of the *pāśasūtra*; the examination of dreams; the procedure for sacrifice (*yāga*); the attainment of the portion of Rudra (*rudrāṃśāpādana*); and the purification of the five *kalās*.

It is unsurpassed—that is, most excellent—even compared to the performance of ritual acts consisting of the entire sequence of ceremonies beginning with the *yojanika*, the instruction, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*), and ending with the dismissal (*visarjana*). || 18 ||
By this mere knowledge, everything is known through all powers.
Indeed, one becomes a member of the common assembly of the Śākinī clan even without yoga;
one who was ignorant of the ritual rules becomes a knower of the rites with respect to the sacrifice.

By means of this great mantra, he is recognized as belonging to the very self of all the powers (śaktis) of Bhairaveśvara; likewise, even while remaining in the state of worldly emergence (vyutthāna) without formal yoga, he is common to the host of Yoginīs, that is, he is shared in common with the entire assembly of Śākinīs.

He shall become a playful child. Even one who previously did not know the ritual procedure becomes a knower of the rules for initiation and sacrifice through the mere knowledge of this great mantra. || 20 ||
Beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Māyā, which resides within the body of Brahmā; Śiva, who extends from Viśva to Ananta, is considered the supreme triad of powers (śaktitraya).

The pervasion of the *nivṛtti-kalā* extends from the tips of the feet to the ankles; therein resides the element of earth (*bhūta-tattva*), and Brahmā holds authority. The pervasion of *pratiṣṭhā* extends from the ankles to the navel;
therein, beginning from the element of water up to the element of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*), the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) reside. In that [region],...

The jurisdiction belongs to Viṣṇu. The pervasion of Vidyā extends from the navel to the palate; therein, the seven principles (tattvas) exist, beginning with the Puruṣa-tattva and ending with the Māyā-tattva, and therein Rudra holds jurisdiction. The pervasion of Śāntā-kalā extends from the palate to the Bindu; therein, the triad of principles beginning with Śuddhavidyā is situated.
In that regard, there is the domain of Īśvara.
There are seven principles (tattvas): Puruṣa, Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, Kalā, and Māyā; three principles known as Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; and the five elements (bhūtas).

There are five sense organs, five organs of action, five objects, three internal organs, and one primordial nature (prakṛti). In the Nivṛtti-kalā there are one hundred and eight worlds; in the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā, fifty-six;
in the Vidyā-kalā, twenty-seven; in the Śāntā-kalā, seventeen; and in the Śāntyatītā-kalā, sixteen.

Thus, all the worlds [number] two hundred and twenty-four. The pervasion of the *bindu* of the *śāntyatītā* [kalā] extends to the end of the aperture of the crown (*karandhra*). Therein resides the *śivatattva* pervaded by Ananta;
therein lies the domain (*adhikṛti*) of Anāśrita Śiva. However, this sequence is presented here only in brief. [From there, it reaches] Kālāgni...

The locus of the Kālāgni [tattva] is the tip of the foot; starting from that point and extending up to the end of Māyā—that is, up to the limit of the Māyā-tattva—the term "Brahman" is used as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa). By this, it is meant that [the state] resides within the bodies of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, reaching as far as the palate.
The reading "brahma" is in the neuter gender. Śiva is above Māyā.

The presiding deity stands as the one who governs from Viśva up to Ananta—that is, beginning from the worlds of Viśva and Śuddhavidyā and extending to the limit of the world of Ananta. Beyond this, the triad of powers—Vidyā, Śāntā, and Śāntyatītā—is considered subtle and supreme. (21)
Why is this so? He says:
"Whatever exists within that, established on the pure path—the individual soul (aṇu)—quickly attains the purified, divine knowledge. (22)

That form of the *adhva* (the path) which exists within those three powers (*śaktitraya*), situated amidst the categories (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and states (*avasthā*) and so forth, is established upon the Pure Path (*śuddhamārga*).
Therein, on the Pure Path, the individual soul (*aṇu-jīva*), through the progressive attenuation of the turbidity of *māyā*, practices yoga.
Established therein, one soon attains the pure, divine knowledge that is free from the manifestation of duality.

The six paths (ṣaḍadhvan)—consisting of phonemes (varṇa), words (pada), mantras, worlds (bhuvana), principles (tattva), and energies (kalā)—comprise three signifiers (vācaka) and three signifieds (vācya). || 22 ||
He who impels that [universe] is to be known as Śiva, the omniscient Supreme Lord;
he is all-pervading, stainless, clear, satisfied, self-abiding, and pure. (23)

The "impeller" (codaka) of that [knowledge] is the one who impels that knowledge of the Lord, the recipient of grace, the motivator toward a certain preeminent yogi; he is to be known as being presided over by a portion of Śiva's power (śivakalā), for he alone is omniscient.
As it has been said:

"He by whom one single entity is seen in its true nature has seen all entities in their true nature. Thus, the Supreme Lord is capable of giving even that which cannot be given; he is all-pervading and omnipresent. Being all-pervading, he is free from the impurity of *māyīya*; being pure, he is free from the impurity of *āṇava*; and being satisfied, he is free from the impurity of *kārmika*.

Free from desire, established in his own abode within the conscious Self, pure and clothed in nothingness—there is no other god like him. The definition of the three impurities (*mala*) is given in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"The loss of sovereignty of consciousness, and the lack of consciousness regarding sovereignty."
This impurity consists of two kinds of atoms, due to the loss of one's own true nature.

"Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is that which is called Māyā, bestowing birth and experience; while Karma belongs to the agent when there is lack of awakening. By the power of Māyā alone, this triad [exists]. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 3.2.4). || 23 ||

Now, it might be argued that for the atomic individual soul (*jīva*), which is contracted, the attainment of the full, all-pervading knowledge of the Lord is difficult to accomplish— just as it is impossible for a drop of water to attain the state of the ocean; therefore, he provides a correct understanding through the illustration of an example:
Just as a great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of a banyan tree,
so too does this entire world of moving and non-moving beings reside within the seed of the heart.

(p. 14) Just as in the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree—the seed of the banyan tree—the power (*śakti*) exists in the form of the heart-seed (*hṛdayabīja*), which consists of the supreme form that is the reflective awareness of pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*). Within that [seed], the entire universe consisting of the moving and the non-moving resides; though it is vast, it remains in a subtle form within the heart-seed. Therefore, it is not [separate from it].
Something is inconsistent. || 24 ||
Thus, for one who knows this in its true essence, initiation leading to nirvāṇa occurs without doubt, even though it is devoid of oblations of sesame and clarified butter.

He who knows— that is, perceives— by way of reality (tattvena), through the casting aside of the ego-identification with the body, and by being established in the conscious Self; "initiation" (dīkṣā) is so called because it bestows the true state of knowledge and destroys all impurity (mala).
Initiation, characterized by the giving [of grace] and the destruction [of bonds], is said to occur through the penetration of awakening.
Characterized by such [qualities], it brings about liberation; thus, disregarding external requisites such as sesame seeds and clarified butter, there is no doubt in this matter. || 25 ||
Having thus described the internal, subtle worship, he also states an illustration of external worship:
"In the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and likewise in the body."
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and tied the topknot (śikhā) consecrated twenty-seven times with the mantra. || 26 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra: "Salutation to the head of Īśāna, salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa, salutation to the heart of Aghora,

salutation to the secret part of Vāmadeva, salutation to the form of Sadyojāta," and having consecrated [the rosary] twenty-seven times with the Aghora mantra using one-quarter of a hundred-and-eight-bead rosary;
Having tied the topknot. || 26 ||
One should perform the binding of each of the ten directions individually,
having first struck three claps with sound for the pacification of obstacles.
With ten snaps of the fingers:
"May the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and reptiles—
all of them— depart, struck by the divine weapon!"
With this mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions:
"May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva."
Having first performed three strikes with the heel while reciting this mantra:
"May those beings who cause heresy, whether they dwell in the earth, the intermediate space,
or reside in the heavenly world, perish by the command of Śiva."
Thus, having made three claps with sound for the sake of pacifying obstacles. || 27 ||
Then, one should sprinkle with water over which the Śikhā-mantra has been recited many times all the offerings,
such as flowers and so forth, in due order, upon either the Liṅga or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The preparation of the seat is performed with a flower consecrated fourteen times.
Having prepared water consecrated twenty-seven times with the Aghora mantra in the weapon-vessel (astrārghapātra) located in the southwest,
one should sprinkle the ritual implements for worship— such as flowers, perfumes, and unbroken rice grains— with the Knowledge-Limb (jñānāṅga) mantra.

One should sprinkle [the object] for the purpose of purification. Then, one should perform the worship beginning with the "flower-seat" (puṣpāsana) upon a clay liṅga or the like, on a sacrificial ground, or on a prepared eight-petalled lotus and so forth, or on the reflection in a mirror, using a flower consecrated fourteen times with the Aghora mantra. || 18 ||
Then the hero should worship the Emanation (Sṛṣṭi), and thereafter the Seat (Āsana) once again.
Having encapsulated the creation (*sṛṣṭi*), one should begin the worship again.

Then, following the external worship, one should worship the creation of the phonemes from *a* to *ha*, and worship them upon the *liṅga* and other supports with the formula "aṃ namaḥ" and so forth. Thus once more, the heroic lord of yogins—

Having assumed the posture for meditative yoga (*dhyānayogāsana*), having encapsulated the creation from *a* to *ha*, and having withdrawn [the senses], one should become established in the consciousness-principle (*cittattva*) as "I" (*aham*), and then begin the internal worship (*antarī pūjā*). The internal worship is precisely the self-reflection (*ātma-amarsana*). 29.
Then, through meditative cultivation, there is worship: [the goddess] perfectly complete with all the principles (*tattva*) and adorned with all ornaments. (30)
One should worship the Goddess Maheśānī with twenty-seven mantras;
thereafter, one should honor her with fragrant flowers according to one's ability.
One should worship with supreme devotion and offer oneself as well;

[one should worship] the Great Goddess, the Supreme Lady, who is perfectly complete and replete with all the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), adorned with every ornament, by means of the Aghora mantra with supreme devotion.
One should worship with devotion and great reverence using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and one should offer oneself—that is, dedicate oneself—to Him. || 31 ||
Thus has the sacrifice been described; this same procedure applies to the fire-ritual as well.
Having properly performed the rite of worship, one attains success by correctly remembering the seed-syllable (*bīja*).

Thus, the two-fold method of sacrifice and worship has been described; this same procedure applies even to fire-rituals such as *homa* and the like, for this very twofold method is as stated. In this manner, the yogi who has performed the rite of worship correctly...

Having forgotten the egoity of the body, by constantly and incessantly remembering and reflecting upon the *cittattva*— the seed and the root cause of the world and its constituent colors— even during states of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*), one attains perfection and ascends to the unsurpassed stream of knowledge. || 32 ||

Now, he states the secret instruction regarding the recollection [of the mantra] in its various forms for the yogi who is established in the yoga of meditation: "The seed-syllable, devoid of beginning and end, situated in the midst of the expanding lunar day (tithi). (33)
One should meditate upon that which resides within the heart-lotus; one should constantly practice the portion of the Moon.
It is the seed-syllable of the world or of the letters, the supreme form, whose essence is consciousness—the reality that is my seed within all beings.
Thus it is stated in the *Gītā*. "Blossoming" (*vikasat*) means expanding from the letter *a* to the letter *ha*;
being rootless, that [expansion] is to be known through its sequence.
In this context, [the letters], having been cognized, transform into the form of consonants within the speech of *vaikharī*.

As these fifteen vowels become clearly manifest, one should meditate upon that which lies within their midst—the "I" (aham)—as non-different from oneself, not as an object of meditation, situated within the heart-lotus; the knower of Rājayoga should practice this through the instruction of the Guru, for the Guru is the means. (Śivasūtra 2.9)
Thus it has been said. And so the Śruti states:
"For the sake of realizing that, one should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) and established in Brahman.
To the question "How should one meditate?", he says: "Devoid of beginning and end"—meaning devoid of the first and last letters among the phonemes (varṇa).
Because it consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). It is also stated in the *Spanda*:
"Of that which arises from the mass of sounds... (*Spanda-kārikā* 4.15). One should meditate in such a way that it becomes free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*).
The intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa), following the sequence of forms assumed by the intellect (buddhi) alone.
Having thus turned back from speech characterized by the middle [state], one should reflect with being (*sattva*).
As it is said in the *Śrīpūrva*:
"This very 'I' consists of the emission (*visarga*) and the unsurpassed (*anuttara*)."
We yogins worship the "I" (Aham) from the space of the heart, which is like an earring upon the navel-pool.
Thus, this indeed is the defining characteristic of non-conceptual meditation (*nirvikalpa-dhyāna*). Through the power of meditative yoga,

preceded by the piercing of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), when the flood of consciousness-bliss suddenly arises like a flash of lightning from the tips of the feet up to the aperture of Brahma (*karandhra*) due to the dissolution of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths within the *suṣumnā*, that very immersion [in it] is [the goal].
"Meditation otherwise is merely hypocritical conduct. Regarding this, he states the method for the application of mindfulness during emergence from samādhi:

"The lunar portion," meaning one should constantly and without interruption practice at the end of the prāṇa when it is about to enter the apāna; that is, one should contemplate the true nature of consciousness (cittattva).
There is no part of the individual soul existing within the two-fold continuum in which the pervasive Śiva-power is not present as its presiding authority.
Thus it has been said. As stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"When the prāṇa has set and the apāna is about to rise, by resorting to external kumbhaka for a long time, one no longer grieves. (Vāsiṣṭha, 6th Prakarana).
Likewise: "We worship the Self of Consciousness, which stands at the end of the state where prāṇa ceases, which reaches the limit where apāna ceases, and which lies between apāna and prāṇa."

Thus it is said. Also in the *Tantrāloka*: "Austerity and the rest, as well as the various observances (*niyama*) and their respective postures (*āsana*), and the breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*)—all of this is merely an external manifestation."
It is stated in the illustrious *Vīrāvali*: "When the moon and the sun have dissolved through the bond of the dissolution of the mind into that which is pure consciousness and of the nature of Śiva,"
When the twelfth part has been reached and the Sun of Life (jīvāditya) is well-awakened, that alone is said to be liberation; [otherwise], breath control (prāṇāyāma) is useless.
"Prāṇāyāma should not be performed by which the body is afflicted" (Tattvārthasūtra 4.1).
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), austerity (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) constitute *kriyāyoga*.

The eight limbs are restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*).
The [terms] beginning with "gāni" and "yogasya" are those taught in the Yogaśāstra. || 33 ||
Whatever desires one may long for, those very desires one shall swiftly obtain. || 34 ||
From this, omniscience becomes manifest; of this there is no doubt. (p.
19) Through this very practice of the supreme reality, one attains—that is, brings into manifestation—the direct perception of desires free from longing. || 34 ||
Thus is the attainment of the fruit of mantra; this is the Rudrayāmala. || 35 ||
Through the practice of this, the perfection of omniscience is attained.

Thus, by means of the two-fold worship, [one attains] the *yāmala*—the form consisting of the union of both—of those two, Rudra and Rudrāṇī, that is, Śiva and Śakti. Perfection is both external and internal.
And it has been said:
"When the mind is restrained within dharma and adharma, whatever he speaks at that time becomes a mantra; how much more so [a mantra] arising from a master of mantras?"
Thus it is said. And so the Śruti declares:
"O Speech, whether uttered or unuttered, be auspicious and most peaceful;
O Sarasvatī, be very gracious, so that thy void may not be seen."

O Sarasvatī, O power whose nature is supreme awareness, inseparable from the Supreme Brahman—you who have arisen as the form of speech, consisting of the awareness of consciousness, manifesting through the state of *vaikharī*; you who, being unarisen in the form of *madhyamā*, are imperceptible to others; and you who are auspicious (*śivā*).
The aspiration is as follows: "May you—who are of the nature of *paśyantī*, free from contact with suffering due to being intent upon the self-reflection of the conscious self (*cidātman*);

and who are most peaceful, the supreme form consisting of the mass of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*)—be very gracious (*sumṛlīkā*) to us, having manifested the extraordinary bliss of consciousness. Likewise, [this applies] to you.

May I not behold—that is, may I not perceive—the "hole" in my own nature, characterized by the forgetting of the awareness of the conscious Self (cidātman), even within the four states; rather, we pray that through the direct realization of Your true nature, I may remain eternally unswerving from it. 35.
I bow to that Cause of all causes, who, covering his single face, himself ordains the creation of the worlds;
who, concealing his own fourteen arms, is expert in the act of protection;
and who, hiding his twelve eyes, destroys [the world] in an instant.
We praise the Lord Svacchanda, who delights in the welfare of others.
Having observed this difficulty in the treatise composed by Guptapāda,
this commentary on the *Triśikā* has been composed by Rājānaka Alasa.
Thus, may there be peace.
Thus ends the *Parātrīśikā-laghuvivṛti* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma.
May it be for the spiritual welfare of both the reader and the scribe.
